Saints levels 13-15 of 23: level 13 is new (Francis Xavier's missionary reach, the accommodation debate, the shared 1622 canonization, 1927 co-patronage of missions with Therese). Level 14 is new (Vincent de Paul and the Daughters of Charity, John Vianney's confessional ministry and patronage of parish priests). Level 15 carries old live level 4's Therese of Lisieux content forward (renumbered, re-seeded) with new material on Story of a Soul, her 1997 Doctor declaration, and the 'shower of roses.' CCC 828/2444/2015/2011/2317 and magisterial_document citations already reviewed are reused throughout.

questions.prompt: St. Francis Xavier, one of the original companions of St. Ignatius of Loyola, is remembered chiefly for what missionary work in the 16th century?
choices: Carrying the Gospel to India and Japan, opening a new era of missionary expansion into Asia
Leading the Council of Trent's own doctrinal deliberations in person
Founding the very first medieval university anywhere in Europe
Personally translating the entire Bible into the Mandarin Chinese language
questions.correctAnswer: Carrying the Gospel to India and Japan, opening a new era of missionary expansion into Asia
questions.explanation: Xavier's mission opened an era of Jesuit missionary work across Asia, raising real, difficult questions about how far local custom could be adapted without compromising the faith -- questions Church History's own treatment of the Chinese and Malabar Rites controversies explores in full.
questions.hint: This missionary's own feast day, December 3, honors work done specifically in Asia.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: True or False: Francis Xavier died on his own journey toward mainland China, never reaching the country he most hoped to evangelize.
questions.explanation: True. Xavier died on an island off the Chinese coast in 1552, still trying to gain entry into China itself -- a real, unfinished ambition at the end of a life already spent evangelizing across thousands of miles of Asia.
questions.hint: Consider whether his final missionary goal was actually reached before his death.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: What made missionary work in this period, unlike in the age of the apostles, a genuinely global undertaking?
choices: European exploration had newly opened sea routes to Asia and the Americas, reaching lands unknown to the ancient and medieval Church
The Roman Empire had, by this later period, somehow expanded to include the whole of Asia directly
All prior missionary activity had, in fact, completely stopped for many centuries before this point
The apostles themselves had already personally evangelized every single one of these same lands centuries earlier
questions.correctAnswer: European exploration had newly opened sea routes to Asia and the Americas, reaching lands unknown to the ancient and medieval Church
questions.explanation: This is a genuinely new missionary situation -- not a repeat of the apostolic-era spread this topic opened with, but an expansion into lands the ancient and medieval Church had no real access to at all.
questions.hint: Consider what specifically changed about Europe's own reach into the wider world in this period.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: Xavier's missionary strategy in Japan involved learning the local language and adapting his approach to Japanese culture, an early example of the ____ debate Church History's own treatment of the Chinese Rites explores in full.
questions.explanation: This same real tension -- how far can missionary method adapt to local culture -- runs through this whole era of missionary sainthood, not only through Matteo Ricci's later, more famous case in China.
questions.hint: The same word Church History uses for Ricci's own missionary method in China.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: True or False: St. Francis Xavier and St. Ignatius of Loyola were canonized on the very same day in 1622, alongside Teresa of Ávila and Philip Neri.
questions.explanation: True. This same shared 1622 canonization, already covered in the previous levels' treatment of Ignatius and Teresa, includes Xavier as well -- four major figures of a single generation's response to the era's crises, recognized together.
questions.hint: Recall the shared canonization date already covered several levels back in this topic.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: In 1927, Pope Pius XI declared Francis Xavier, alongside St. Thérèse of Lisieux, co-patron of what?
choices: Missionary work, in recognition of two very different paths to the same missionary heart
The Papal States, restored to their pre-1870 borders
The Society of Jesus alone, to the exclusion of Thérèse's own religious community
The Roman Curia's internal administrative offices
questions.correctAnswer: Missionary work, in recognition of two very different paths to the same missionary heart
questions.explanation: Xavier traveled tens of thousands of miles across Asia; Thérèse, covered several levels ahead in this topic, never left her Carmelite convent -- yet the Church recognizes both as living the same missionary heart in radically different circumstances.
questions.hint: One of these two patrons traveled across continents; the other never left her convent.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about St. Francis Xavier to what it involves.

pairs.right: The lands Xavier's own missionary journeys reached
The year Xavier was canonized alongside Ignatius and Teresa
Declared co-patron of missionary work alongside Thérèse of Lisieux

questions.explanation: Xavier's own arc -- vast geographic reach, an unfinished ambition, and a lasting institutional legacy recognized centuries later -- shows missionary sainthood as real, costly, and genuinely unfinished even at its most celebrated.
questions.hint: Follow Xavier's own arc: where he went, where he died still trying to reach, and how the Church later honored him twice.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: True or False: Missionary saints of this era, including Xavier, sometimes worked alongside colonial powers whose own conduct the Church has since acknowledged included real injustice.
questions.explanation: True, and this level does not pretend otherwise -- Church History's own treatment of the Crusades and the missions already models this same honesty: real holiness and real complicated political context can coexist in a single era without either canceling the other out.
questions.hint: Recall Church History's own honest treatment of complicated political context in this same period.

citations.quote: Injustice, excessive economic or social inequalities, envy, distrust, and pride raging among men and nations constantly threaten peace and cause wars.

questions.prompt: Xavier is traditionally remembered as having baptized more converts personally than any other missionary since the ____, an era this topic's own earliest levels covered.
questions.explanation: This comparison deliberately ties Xavier's own missionary reach back to level 2's apostles -- the same pattern of costly, wide-ranging witness this topic opened with, now unfolding again on an even larger geographic scale.
questions.hint: The same generation this topic's own level 2 covered, many levels back.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: Given this level's picture of missionary sainthood abroad, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: Saints of charity closer to home -- Vincent de Paul and John Vianney, answering the needs of ordinary parish life
A complete repeat of this same level's material about Francis Xavier
A jump backward to Thomas More's own era, already fully covered
A subject entirely unrelated to sainthood or to the historical period this topic has reached
questions.correctAnswer: Saints of charity closer to home -- Vincent de Paul and John Vianney, answering the needs of ordinary parish life
questions.explanation: The next level shifts from the missionary frontier back to the ordinary parish -- a different, quieter kind of holiness, no less real for taking place close to home rather than across an ocean.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

citations.quote: By canonizing some of the faithful... the Church recognizes the power of the Spirit of holiness within her and sustains the hope of believers by proposing the saints to them as models and intercessors.

questions.prompt: St. Vincent de Paul, a 17th-century French priest, is remembered chiefly for organizing what kind of work among the poor?
choices: Systematic, organized charity -- founding religious communities dedicated specifically to serving the poor and sick
Missionary work carried out across Asia, in essentially the same pattern as Francis Xavier
Formal doctrinal debate conducted directly against Reformation theology
A broad reform of monastic enclosure rules governing cloistered nuns
questions.correctAnswer: Systematic, organized charity -- founding religious communities dedicated specifically to serving the poor and sick
questions.explanation: Vincent moved beyond individual acts of charity to build lasting institutions -- the Congregation of the Mission and, with St. Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity -- turning personal compassion into organized, sustained service.
questions.hint: His real innovation was building lasting institutions, not just performing individual acts of charity.

questions.prompt: St. Vincent de Paul, with St. Louise de Marillac, founded the ____ of Charity, a community of women religious dedicated to direct service among the poor and sick.
questions.explanation: Unlike earlier cloistered orders such as level 8's Poor Clares, the Daughters of Charity were deliberately designed to work actively in the world -- among the poor, in hospitals and homes, rather than behind convent walls.
questions.hint: The community's full name pairs this word with 'of Charity.'

questions.prompt: True or False: St. John Vianney, the Curé d'Ars, was known for spending extraordinarily long hours each day hearing confessions.
questions.explanation: True. Vianney reportedly spent up to sixteen or more hours a day in the confessional during the height of his ministry, as penitents traveled from across France to seek him out -- an extreme, sustained form of pastoral service few other priests have matched.
questions.hint: Consider what drew penitents from across France to this one small rural parish.

citations.quote: The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross. There is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle.

questions.prompt: St. John Vianney struggled significantly with his seminary studies, particularly Latin, and nearly failed to be ordained at all. What does his eventual sainthood suggest about the relationship between academic gifts and holiness?
choices: Real sanctity does not require exceptional intellectual gifts -- pastoral devotion and prayer can be just as decisive
The Church requires every priest to demonstrate exceptional academic ability before ordination
Vianney's struggles disqualified him from ever being ordained at all
Academic struggle is itself a formal requirement for canonization
questions.correctAnswer: Real sanctity does not require exceptional intellectual gifts -- pastoral devotion and prayer can be just as decisive
questions.explanation: Vianney's ordination was genuinely uncertain given his academic struggles -- his eventual recognition as patron of parish priests is a real, documented case that intellectual brilliance and priestly holiness are not the same thing.
questions.hint: Consider what almost prevented his ordination at all, and what he became famous for instead.

citations.quote: The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross. There is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle.

questions.prompt: True or False: Vincent de Paul's charitable organizing extended to practical relief efforts during periods of war and famine in 17th-century France.
questions.explanation: True. Vincent's communities organized real relief -- food, medical care, and shelter -- during a genuinely brutal period of French wars and famine, showing his charity was concrete and organized, not merely sentimental.
questions.hint: Consider what kind of real, practical crises Vincent's communities actually responded to.

questions.prompt: Match each saint of this level to what makes him one of its figures of charity.

pairs.right: Organized systematic charity for the poor and sick
An active, uncloistered order Vincent co-founded
The Curé d'Ars, known for extraordinary hours in confession
Nearly prevented his ordination, despite his eventual sainthood

questions.explanation: Neither of these two saints founded a global missionary movement or reformed a whole religious order -- their holiness is expressed in patient, unglamorous, day-to-day service, a real and different shape from every founder this topic has covered so far.
questions.hint: Two rows concern Vincent's organized charity; two concern Vianney's own personal, patient ministry.

questions.prompt: True or False: John Vianney is recognized by the Church as the patron saint of parish priests.
questions.explanation: True. This patronage recognizes exactly the kind of holiness his life models -- unglamorous, sustained, daily pastoral service to one small community, rather than a founder's institutional legacy or a missionary's global reach.
questions.hint: Consider what specific vocation his own decades of quiet, patient ministry most directly speaks to.

citations.quote: The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross. There is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle.

questions.prompt: What do Vincent de Paul and John Vianney add to this topic's growing picture of sainthood, compared to the missionary and reforming saints covered in earlier levels?
choices: Holiness expressed through patient, sustained, unglamorous service close to home rather than dramatic founding acts or distant missionary reach
Nothing new -- their paths are functionally identical to Francis Xavier's missionary work covered in the previous level
Proof that only founders of new religious orders can be recognized as saints
A return to the exact martyrdom pattern this topic opened with, with no real difference
questions.correctAnswer: Holiness expressed through patient, sustained, unglamorous service close to home rather than dramatic founding acts or distant missionary reach
questions.explanation: This level deliberately shows a quieter register of sainthood -- neither founding a global order nor traveling to a new continent, but decades of patient, repeated, ordinary service that the Church still recognizes as heroic virtue.
questions.hint: Compare the scale and drama of this level's saints to Francis Xavier's own missionary reach in the previous level.

questions.prompt: St. John Vianney's decades of extraordinary time spent hearing ____ show that sustained, patient, repeated service can itself be a real and recognized path to sainthood.
questions.explanation: No single dramatic act defines Vianney's sainthood -- it is the sheer, sustained repetition of one ordinary priestly duty, carried out for decades, that the Church recognized as heroic.
questions.hint: The sacrament Vianney is most famous for spending extraordinary hours administering.

citations.quote: The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross. There is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle.

questions.prompt: Given this level's quieter picture of sustained, ordinary holiness, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: St. Thérèse of Lisieux's Little Way, holiness found in the smallest and most ordinary of daily acts
A complete repeat of this same level's material about Vincent de Paul and Vianney
A jump backward to Francis Xavier's own missionary era, already fully covered
A subject entirely unrelated to sainthood or to the historical period this topic has reached
questions.correctAnswer: St. Thérèse of Lisieux's Little Way, holiness found in the smallest and most ordinary of daily acts
questions.explanation: The next level continues, and in some ways completes, exactly this level's own theme -- Thérèse's Little Way takes the ordinary, unglamorous holiness this level has just shown and makes it the explicit center of her whole spirituality.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: St. Thérèse of Lisieux described her simple, humble approach to holiness -- trusting God like a child rather than through great deeds -- as her '____ Way.'
questions.explanation: Thérèse taught that small acts of love, offered with total trust, could sanctify anyone -- a spirituality so influential that John Paul II declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1997, despite her short, hidden life.
questions.hint: This spirituality is about small, humble acts rather than heroic ones.

citations.reference: John Paul II, declaring St. Thérèse of Lisieux a Doctor of the Church (1997)

questions.prompt: True or False: St. Thérèse of Lisieux entered the Carmelite convent at the unusually young age of fifteen.
questions.explanation: True. Thérèse required a special papal permission to enter so young -- a real sign of how early and how deeply her sense of vocation had already formed, well before most people her age would consider such a step.
questions.hint: Consider how unusual her age was for entering religious life, even in her own era.

questions.prompt: Thérèse's own account of her life and her Little Way, written at her superior's request and published shortly after her death, is known by what title?
choices: Story of a Soul
The Interior Castle
The Dialogue
The Imitation of Christ
questions.explanation: This short autobiography, never intended for wide publication in Thérèse's own lifetime, became one of the most widely read spiritual works of the modern era -- proof that her 'little' way was never actually small in its eventual reach.
questions.hint: This title names the book's real subject -- not a life of great deeds, but a soul's own inner story.

questions.prompt: True or False: Thérèse of Lisieux died at the age of twenty-four, after a long and painful illness with tuberculosis.
questions.explanation: True. Her whole recognized holiness -- Little Way, autobiography, later Doctor-of-the-Church title -- unfolded within a life barely a quarter-century long, most of it spent behind convent walls unknown to the wider world.
questions.hint: Consider how short her entire life actually was.

questions.prompt: Shortly before her death, Thérèse promised to spend her heaven doing good on earth, letting fall a shower of ____ -- a promise closely tied to her later popular devotion.
questions.explanation: This image gave rise to a widespread popular devotion -- believers reporting a rose, or the scent of roses, as a sign of her intercession -- a striking case of ordinary devotional practice growing up around a genuinely humble, hidden life.
questions.hint: This flower became closely associated with signs of her intercession after death.

questions.prompt: In 1997, Thérèse of Lisieux became the youngest person ever declared a Doctor of the Church, and only the third woman, alongside whom?
choices: Teresa of Ávila and Catherine of Siena, already covered earlier in this topic
Hildegard of Bingen and Joan of Arc
Perpetua and Felicity, covered many levels earlier
No other women had been declared Doctors of the Church before her
questions.correctAnswer: Teresa of Ávila and Catherine of Siena, already covered earlier in this topic
questions.explanation: Both women Doctors this topic has already covered -- Teresa in level 11, Catherine in level 9 -- precede Thérèse, whose own declaration in 1997 makes her the third, and by far the youngest, confirming that the criteria for this title genuinely do not depend on age or length of life.
questions.hint: Both other women Doctors have already appeared earlier in this same topic.

citations.reference: John Paul II, declaring St. Thérèse of Lisieux a Doctor of the Church (1997)

questions.prompt: True or False: Thérèse's Little Way is a lower, easier standard of holiness than the more visibly heroic sanctity of saints like the martyrs or the great founders.
questions.explanation: False. Trusting entirely in God's mercy rather than one's own visible achievement is, for many people, considerably harder than a program of dramatic effort -- the Little Way is not an easier bar, only a different, more hidden one.
questions.hint: Consider whether total trust, with no visible achievement to point to, is actually easier than heroic effort.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about St. Thérèse of Lisieux to what it involves.

pairs.right: Holiness through small, trusting acts of love, not heroic deeds
Her autobiography, published shortly after her death
Her entire recognized holiness unfolded in a very short life
Declared the youngest Doctor of the Church

questions.explanation: Every fact in this level points the same direction -- a short, hidden, outwardly unremarkable life recognized as one of the most influential spiritualities in the modern Church.
questions.hint: Follow her own short arc: her spirituality, her book, her death, and her eventual title.

citations.reference: John Paul II, declaring St. Thérèse of Lisieux a Doctor of the Church (1997)

questions.prompt: What does Thérèse's case add to this topic's picture of sainthood, taken together with the quiet, sustained holiness of Vincent de Paul and Vianney in the previous level?
choices: That real holiness can be found in the smallest, most hidden circumstances, not only in visible founding acts or public witness
That only saints with a long public ministry, like Vincent de Paul, can ever be recognized as truly holy
That Thérèse's own path is, in the end, functionally identical to Francis Xavier's global missionary reach
That living a short life automatically disqualifies someone from ever being recognized as a Doctor of the Church
questions.correctAnswer: That real holiness can be found in the smallest, most hidden circumstances, not only in visible founding acts or public witness
questions.explanation: This is the real thread connecting levels 14 and 15: sainthood does not require a global stage, a founded institution, or even a long life -- small, hidden faithfulness is itself a complete and recognized path.
questions.hint: Consider what Vincent, Vianney, and Thérèse all share, despite their very different circumstances.

questions.prompt: Given this level's picture of hidden 19th-century holiness, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: Missionary and founder saints of the wider 19th century, beyond Thérèse's own hidden convent life
A complete repeat of this same level's material about Thérèse
A jump backward to Vincent de Paul's own era, already fully covered
A subject entirely unrelated to sainthood or to the historical period this topic has reached
questions.correctAnswer: Missionary and founder saints of the wider 19th century, beyond Thérèse's own hidden convent life
questions.explanation: The next level widens the lens again -- from one hidden Carmelite's short life to the broader missionary and institutional expansion of sainthood across the rest of the 19th century.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.
